extracted.intended_audience: steamship captains, pilots, navigators, traders and hydrographers operating on the Upper Amazon and its tributaries
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and operational standards for navigating the Upper Amazon and its principal tributaries: seasonal regimes, depths, currents, hazards, chart usage, port characteristics, fuel and cargo handling for steamers and boats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal rise and fall awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: The waters of the Upper Amazon and its tributaries begin to rise annually in October, remain stationary for a short time in December, continue to rise until May, and then commence to fall. November–April are months of high water; June–September are low-water season; October and May are sometimes high and sometimes low.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan voyages, cargo loads, and route choices around these seasonal regimes because navigability, currents, and risk of grounding change substantially between high and low seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum channel depth requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: During low water a minimum depth of 24 feet is found in the channel of the Upper Amazon from the Brazilian frontier to the mouth of the Ucayali; 18 feet from the mouth of the Ucayali to the mouth of the Huallaga; and 12 feet from the mouth of the Huallaga to Borja (head of practical navigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these minimum depths to determine vessel draught limits and cargo loading plans; sections with less depth will limit how large a steamer can safely proceed at low water.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know average current speeds and their variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Average currents are given by stretches (e.g., 3 mph from Brazilian frontier to Ucayali mouth; 3.25 mph from Ucayali mouth to Potro mouth; up to 3.75 mph toward Borja). Currents increase or diminish with rise/fall of the river and with narrowing or broadening of the channel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate average current speeds into voyage timing and engine/fuel planning, and expect deviations when water levels or channel geometry change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experienced local pilots
rubrics_metrics.description: To prevent running upon sand-bars, which are constantly forming and shifting and frequently changing the bed of the channel, the services of experienced pilots are indispensable to the safe navigation of the Upper Amazon and its tributaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure local, experienced pilots (often expert hunters and fishermen) for safe passage; hiring them is standard practice and they are usually available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer navigation during rising water
rubrics_metrics.description: Navigation of the Amazon is attended with much less difficulty when the waters of the river are rising than when they are falling. Getting aground when the water is falling may detain a vessel until the next rise (months); grounding when the water is rising usually necessitates only a few hours' delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schedule critical passages for rising-water periods where possible; avoid trying to pass shallow stretches during the falling season.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuel logistics: wood as primary fuel
rubrics_metrics.description: Coal is not to be found on the Upper Amazon; steamers burn wood, which is abundant and cheap and makes good fuel. Wood should be ordered in advance at certain points, but if a steamer gives out of fuel the crew can cut wood ashore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan fuel supply ahead (pre-order wood at known points), store adequate reserves, and ensure crew and equipment are prepared to procure wood if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cargo transfer and port handling without wharves
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of wharves on the Upper Amazon and its tributaries, vessels lay alongside of the banks whilst discharging or receiving cargo. The banks at the usual stopping places afford good landings; wharves are not needed and would be difficult to construct for all stages of the water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize cargo operations to be done from ships alongside banks; choose stopping places with good high-bank landings and prepare for beach/shore-based loading and unloading procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accurate charts and appropriate scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Charts and plans are drawn at specific scales (examples: one inch to two miles; one inch to ten or fifteen miles) and on multiple sheets covering long river reaches; detailed and larger-scale charts show the same surveys more in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on hydrographical charts of appropriate scale for the stretch to be navigated; carry both detailed (large-scale) and overview (small-scale) charts to plan and execute passages safely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the head of navigation and major impassable obstacles
rubrics_metrics.description: Borja is the head of steamer navigation; from Laracocha to Borja the river is a mountain torrent impracticable for navigation even by canoes. Rapids, falls and the pongo de Manseriche render further navigation impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan journeys with awareness of absolute limits (e.g., Borja); do not expect steamer navigation beyond certain rapids/ponchos, and factor in required transshipment or overland routes where navigation ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and prepare for specific hazardous passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain passages (e.g., Vuelta Calentura/Calentura passage) present strong currents combined with whirlpools; narrow points (e.g., Tamshiyacu) create strong currents and may be the only practical places to interdict navigation militarily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach known hazardous points with full steam, local pilotage, and caution; plan for additional time and power when passing whirlpools, strong currents, or narrow channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand tributary navigability and inter-river connections
rubrics_metrics.description: Tributaries have differing depths and navigable reaches (e.g., Ucayali carries 24 ft from Nauta to Sarayacu, 18 ft to Pachitea mouth, 12 ft to Tambo–Urubamba confluence). Some tributaries (Tambo) are likely navigable for steamers drawing 8–10 ft to certain points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose vessel and loading according to specific tributary depth limits; use tributary navigability data to plan routes to interior posts and potential Pacific connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Port-specific characteristics for anchorage and trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Ports differ: Iquitos has good anchorage at all times and high banks for safe alongside laying; Nauta is well located for trade at Ucayali mouth though requires ascending the Amazon a few miles; Yurimaguas is a trade center connecting steamers and interior routes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select stopping points based on anchorage, bank conditions, and connectivity; use Iquitos for secure cargo operations and Yurimaguas as transfer hub to interior routes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade and provisioning knowledge for commercial planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Local import demands: coarse cotton cloth (American preferred), wheat flour (Baltimore/Richmond brands), axes, hoes, spades, machetes, some firearms, ready-made clothing and furniture. Exports include Panama hats, rum, dried fish, and India rubber; bacon spoils quickly in climate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan cargo inventory and provisioning to match local demand and perishability; be cautious about transporting perishable goods like bacon and prefer in-demand items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use published distances and steaming times for voyage planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed lists of distances between places on the Amazon and its tributaries are provided (e.g., Iquitos to Borja usually takes 69 steaming hours to ascend and 35 to descend). Distances for Lower and Upper Amazon are drawn from different authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate published mileages and typical steaming hours into scheduling, fuel and provisioning calculations, and connection timing with inland routes.
